extraction.methodology_summary: The paper develops a deep learning statistical arbitrage framework by first constructing arbitrage portfolios as residuals from conditional latent asset pricing factors (Fama-French, PCA, or IPCA). Second, time series signals are extracted from these residual portfolios using a convolutional transformer architecture combining local convolutional filters and attention-based global dependency modeling. Finally, these signals are mapped into an optimal trading allocation via a nonparametric feedforward neural network that maximizes risk-adjusted returns under trading constraints.
extraction.universe: Roughly the 550 largest and most liquid U.S. common stocks from CRSP with market capitalization larger than 0.01% of the total market capitalization

key_findings: The deep learning statistical arbitrage model (CNN+Transformer) substantially outperforms all benchmark approaches out-of-sample, achieving annual Sharpe ratios greater than four.
Signal extraction is the most challenging and critical component of statistical arbitrage, whereas the specific choice of asset pricing factor models has a secondary effect.
Arbitrage trading signals are persistent over short horizons, with about half of the Sharpe ratio surviving for a holding period of one week, and remaining profitable over a one-month holding period.
The convolutional transformer network learns asymmetric policies, reacting quickly to downturn movements while acting more cautiously during uptrends.
Arbitrage strategies remain highly profitable and economically significant even after accounting for realistic transaction and holding costs.
limitations: The empirical evaluation is restricted to the largest and most liquid U.S. equities, avoiding broader market frictions and liquidity issues associated with small-cap stocks.
The study assumes linear proportional transaction and holding costs in the friction extension rather than modeling full endogenous market impact.
Network rolling window training and periodic re-estimation introduce computational complexity and approximations.
